https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Emergency responders clear rubble from a Kyiv apartment block attacked by Russian drones on Sunday. Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPA View image in fullscreen Emergency responders clear rubble from a Kyiv apartment block attacked by Russian drones on Sunday. Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPA Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Moscow terrorising Ukrainians as fresh strikes kill eight Ukraine president says Russia shows no signs of slowing the war, calls for sanctions packages to take effect in October. What we know on day 1,678 Guardian staff and agencies Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.15 EDT Last modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google As Russian drones struck Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was showing no signs of de-escalating the war despite assurances to the US that it would . In a statement on X, Zelenskyy accused Russia of terrorising Ukrainians with its latest attacks, which he said included setting on fire a market outside Kyiv, and striking kindergartens, schools, homes and communications facilities. “Anywhere in the world, this choice of targets would be called by one word – terrorism. Russia has no military objective whatsoever in doing this – it is purely an attempt to break people and inflict as much harm as possible on our society,” Zelenskyy said. “If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps toward de-escalation – as it claims, particularly to American negotiators – this wave of … terror would not be happening,” he said, calling on the US to fully implement the Lindsey Graham Act, which enables sweeping sanctions on Russia aimed at pressing it into ending the war. Zelenskyy’s comments came ahead of the conclusion of the UN general assembly in New York on Monday. On the weekend, the foreign ministers of Russia and Germany met in New York on the sidelines of the ⁠assembly to discuss the war but Russia’s top diplomat dismissed Germany’s calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” towards Europe. Zelenskyy said on X that Ukraine was relying on “effective decisions” being made by other countries and stronger pressure from its partners in the G7 and G20 , “so that Russia sees that manipulating diplomatic signals will not allow it to keep winning more and more time for war and terror”. New sanctions packages targeting financial networks, supply chains and companies and individuals helping produce Russian weapons “must take effect as early as October” Zelenskyy said also, to provide a stronger foundation for changing the situation and “pushing Russia toward real diplomacy”. Russian strikes killed eight people across Ukraine on Sunday , according to authorities while Zelenskyy said Russia had fired about 3,900 drones, aerial bombs and other missiles at Ukraine over the past week. Ukrainian prosecutors said a drone attack hit a market in Sofiiska Borshchahivka on the western outskirts of Kyiv, killing two and injuring about 10 people. Others died in strikes in different regions and Kyiv also came under attack, local officials said. In the capital, ⁠Mayor Vitali Klitschko said nine people were injured, including a child. Russia hit also the headquarters of Kyivstar, Ukraine’s largest mobile service provider on Sunday , the company told local media, as Moscow continued a bombardment of Ukrainian ⁠datacentres and communications infrastructure. Kyivstar told Interfax Ukraine news agency that its head office in Kyiv had been hit, but there were no casualties. Peter Beaumont and Artem Mazhulin have reported on the dire living conditions inside Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson . Life in the city – once home to 24,000 people but now with only 2,000 remaining – has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there. South ⁠Korea has demanded an official ⁠explanation and apology ​from Ukraine , accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea and then falsely denying that the two sides had agreed to keep the move ⁠confidential, according to a report from Reuters. “The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement,” Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement on Sunday. According to the statement, President Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer in his address to the UN general assembly. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. https://www.politico.eu/article/spains-c.text: The leader of Spain’s conservative People’s Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, confirmed Tuesday that he is negotiating with the far right ahead of the Nov. 29 snap election to secure a majority in the Senate. “Vox knows how far we can go; they know we have a sense of state,” Feijóo said Tuesday morning in an interview on Spanish radio station COPE , alluding to an alliance with the far-right party. “It would be a mistake to hand control over to Sanchismo ,” he added, in reference to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist government. Feijóo, who is eyeing the premiership, said he was negotiating with Vox to coordinate Senate lists and counter a potential coalition between the governing socialists and other left-wing parties. Advertisement Advertisement “We are going to continue talking to Vox with discretion and respect. If Vox is up to the task, the PP will also be up to the task,” he said, adding that the two parties were working on a deal to not compete with each other in key areas to ensure a conservative majority in the upper house of the Spanish parliament. Feijóo’s comments echo those of Vox leader Santiago Abascal the day before: He said in a statement Monday he would negotiate with the People’s Party to prevent Sánchez from “stealing the elections,” accusing him of sowing “coercion and violence” to influence the vote. “Sánchez’s alliance with the far left demands sacrifices from the opposition parties, and we remain willing to reach some kind of agreement that protects the Senate from the deals Sánchez has struck with the far left,” he said. In a blow to the Socialist prime minister, the left wing has failed to unite ahead of November’s election, with prominent party Podemos opting out of a broad, joint ticket except in the Canary Islands and the Valencia region.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: View image in fullscreen Russia’s war dead Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict Composite: Getty Images/EPA/Guardian/Guardian design Exclusive: Analysis gives most detailed picture yet of the nearly 500,000 Russian losses in Ukraine since 2022 Leaked data shows more than 1,000 Russian military suicides during Ukraine war Pjotr Sauer , Michael Goodier , Harriet Agerholm , Philip McMahon , Lucy Swan and Carmen Aguilar García . Graphics by Heidi Wilson Mon 23 Nov 2026 11.00 EST Last modified on Mon 23 Nov 2026 11.01 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Composite: Getty Images/EPA/Guardian/Guardian design A lexander Korepanov signed up to fight in August 2023. He was wounded twice and twice sent back to the front. On 11 May 2025, after 20 months at war, he was killed in the village of Uspenovka, near the eastern Ukrainian city of Pokrovsk, aged 52. More than 5,000 died with him that week. The Russian army was losing a staggering 720 men every 24 hours, the highest rate of the war, and at least a third of them were killed around Pokrovsk, where Moscow had thrown tens of thousands of troops into its spring offensive. The figure comes from a cache of more than 11m death certificates obtained by the hacking group Cyber Partisans, which is linked to the Belarusian opposition, and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow. Analysed in depth by the Guardian, they give the most detailed picture yet of Russia’s losses in Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Map showing deadly battlefields for Russian military in Ukraine Among them, the Guardian identified more than 460,000 deaths linked to the war between the start of the invasion in February 2022 and September 2026. War became the leading cause of death in Russian men under 65 last year. “There was always sort of an unknown X factor: how many Russian deaths are we missing? And that turned out to be much much more,” said Janis Kluge, a Russia expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, who has closely tracked military deaths. Militaries typically expect about three wounded for every soldier killed. But Kluge said the data suggested Russia could have more soldiers killed in action than severely wounded. “This tells you something about this war and the way that it’s fought,” Kluge said. For all those losses, the frontline has barely moved. Since the start of 2023, Russia has gained about 8,000 sq km, less than 1.5% of Ukraine’s territory, according to data from the Ukrainian monitoring group DeepState. View image in fullscreen A cemetery in Nikolayevka, Russia, which contains the graves of volunteer fighters from the Samara region who have been killed in the war in Ukraine. Photograph: Max Avdeev/The Guardian Stuck on the frontline, Russia has this year turned to destroying Ukraine’s economy and making life in its cities unlivable , in an attempt to force Kyiv into accepting its terms for peace. Russia’s defence ministry has not updated its official death toll since September 2022, when it said 5,937 servicemen had been killed, and Moscow treats its casualty numbers as a military secret. The records analysed by the Guardian, compiled by Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, from civil registry offices across the country, show a war that grew steadily more lethal, peaking dramatically in 2025, with little territorial gain for Moscow. Almost 20,000 deaths were recorded during the first year of the invasion and 50,000 in 2023. In 2024 the toll more than doubled, to more than 134,000 and it rose a further 52% a year later, to close to 200,000, the deadliest year of the war: about 548 men a day, against an average of about 277 since the invasion began. The scale dwarfs anything suffered by Russia or the Soviet Union since the second world war. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers were killed over the nine years of the Soviet war in Afghanistan, according to official figures; in the worst year, 1984, the toll was about 2,300. In Ukraine in 2025, Russia was losing that many men roughly every four days. Graphic showing Russian war deaths by location The comparison with recent western wars is starker still. In the single week that began on 5 May 2025, the Russian army lost more men than the US did in eight years in Iraq, where roughly 4,500 American troops died. About 2,400 US service members perished in two decades in Afghanistan. The real toll is likely to be higher. The deaths of missing soldiers are often registered months or years later, when bodies are recovered or courts declare men dead, and the records thin out sharply in 2026, even though the fighting has remained exceptionally deadly. Nor does the database capture every death, with some never registered or soldiers missing. View image in fullscreen Russian conscripts called up for military service prepare to depart for garrisons from a recruitment centre in Bataysk, Rostov region, May 2024. Photograph: Sergey Pivovarov/Reuters The analysis includes death certificates classified as war-related or where conflict is mentioned as a cause of death – a count which may include some civilians. It also includes all deaths where the employment was marked as military – but excludes any certificates from non-combat age people. The losses are deepening a demographic crisis the Kremlin has struggled for years to reverse, with consequences likely to be felt for generations. In 2025, war became the leading cause of death for men under the age of 65. Of the death certificates with recorded cause, 29% mentioned war, followed by 26% of deaths due to circulatory diseases and 12% from external causes, such as accidents, assaults or medical complications. More than half a million Russians have also left the country since the invasion. “We’ve been predicting demographic doom for Russia for a few decades, and somehow the catastrophe never materialised,” said Judyth Twigg, a professor of global health at Virginia Commonwealth University in the US. “But the current situation really does look qualitatively different … Today’s losses are a direct consequence of regime policy: combat deaths, political emigration, foregone births, healthcare budgets raided to fund [military] signing bonuses and death payouts.” The Pokrovsk meat grinder The certificates record where most soldiers died, down to the village, from mid-2023 onwards. The records show how much Russia has paid for every kilometre gained on a handful of narrow fronts, above all in the slow advance through the fortified mining towns north-west of Donetsk. View image in fullscreen Russian casualties and destroyed armoured vehicles that were attempting to storm Avdivka, in December 2023. Photograph: Kostya Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images Almost 116,000 of the deaths – over a quarter of the total with a known recorded location – occurred in Pokrovsk district, which takes in both Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, scenes of two of the longest and bloodiest battles of the war. Pokrovsk itself, a coalmining town of 60,000 people before the war, covers less than 30 sq km. More Russian soldiers have died in the district around it than Ukrainians lived in the city itself. After neighbouring Avdiivka fell in February 2024 , Russian troops took 21 months to cover 39km (24 miles) to the edge of Pokrovsk, according to the Institute for the Study of War. In that time, about 88,700 Russian soldiers were recorded as dying in the district, more than 2,200 for every kilometre gained. By September 2024, Russia’s gains formed a bulge of fields, slag heaps and mining villages about 30km long and 20km wide. View image in fullscreen A Soviet-era monument dedicated to second world war soldiers stands in front of a destroyed house of culture near Avdiivka, Donetsk region, Ukraine, in March 2024. Photograph: Alex Babenko/AP The rest of the front is traceable through the data too. Recorded deaths in Russia’s Kursk region rose from 12 in July 2024 to close to 1,200 in August, when Ukraine launched its cross-border incursion into the area, and reached more than 2,400 in December as Moscow fought to retake the territory. The losses are eroding Russia’s ability to mount new offensives, and help explain why its army looks set to fail to carry out Putin’s order to capture the whole of the Donbas region by the end of the year. “If we compare the death data with Russia’s official recruitment rates, it becomes clear that Russia’s military has a manpower problem,” said Kluge. “The absolutely horrible losses combined with slower recruitment rates apparently forced Russia to slow down its attacks in 2026 already,” he added. Older men, poorer regions In 2018, Putin spoke of Russians looking forward to a “well-deserved retirement”, when they could devote more time to their families, children and grandchildren. Eight years later, more and more older Russian men are dying on the battlefields of Ukraine. The average age at death has risen from 34 in 2022 to close to 40 this year. Graphic showing Russian war deaths by poverty level Almost a fifth of the soldiers killed in 2026 whose age is recorded were over 50, against 6% in the first year of the war. Across the war, men aged 35 to 44 make up a third of the dead. The shift reflects how Russia has filled its military ranks. Rather than order a second mobilisation – the first, seven months after the start of the full-scale invasion, in September 2022, was deeply unpopular – the Kremlin has relied on cash bonuses to attract volunteers, and the money has often appealed most to older men such as Korepanov. From the start of the war, the Kremlin has sought to keep the cost out of sight in Moscow and St Petersburg, where discontent poses the greatest political risk. View image in fullscreen Young Russian marine recruits attend a departure ceremony to join the army in St Petersburg, June 2024. Photograph: Anatoly Maltsev/EPA The losses fall hardest on Russia’s poor, far-flung regions, many of them home to large ethnic minority populations. The eight Russian regions with the most poverty recorded a military death rate four times higher than those with the least, recording more than 10 deaths per 1,000 men aged 18-69, compared with fewer than three per 1,000. In at least 19 Russian regions, most of them in the far east, more than half of deaths of men under 50 in 2025 were due to the war. The figures are based on place of birth, using records where a cause of death was given. View image in fullscreen A poster of a Russian soldier with a slogan reading ‘Glory to the heroes of Russia’ on a road near a chapel that was built in memory of Wagner fighters near Goryachy Klyuch, Russia, in February 2023. Photograph: Nanna Heitmann/The New York Times/Redux/eyevine In the Jewish autonomous oblast, a region in eastern Russia bordering China where about a fifth of the population lived in poverty in 2022, which despite its Soviet-era name is less than 1% Jewish, war was listed as the cause of more than three-quarters of recorded deaths of men under 50 last year. The highest death rate was recorded in Zabaykalsky Krai, another region bordering China thousands of miles from the front, where about one in six people live below the poverty line. Since the beginning of the war, 32 men aged 18 to 69 born in the region have died per 1,000 population, compared with one per 1,000 in St Petersburg and Moscow, where less than 5% live in poverty. Foreigners at the front As losses have mounted, Moscow has cast its net even wider. Alongside the cash bonuses offered at home, Russia has recruited heavily among central Asian migrant workers inside the country and, through networks of murky middlemen abroad, from as far afield as Nepal, India, Cuba and Kenya. View image in fullscreen Charles Ojiambo Mutoka, 72, holds portraits of his son Oscar, who he learned was killed in August, during a press conference where relatives of conscripts demanded urgent government action to repatriate their family members, in Nairobi in January 2026. Photograph: Tony Karumba/AFP/Getty Images Many recruits were lured by promises of high pay, Russian citizenship or civilian jobs, only to find themselves at the front. The Guardian identified more than 7,300 probable foreign soldiers among the dead, not counting Ukrainians. That includes 2,700 who were born abroad but have no recorded citizenship. Many come from the large central Asian migrant workforce Russia has courted with fast-track citizenship in exchange for service, with more than three-quarters coming from former Soviet republics, mainly from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Belarus. But the analysis identified foreign fighters from 78 other countries beyond the former USSR, including 440 whose citizenship was from an African country – such as Nigeria, Cameroon and Egypt, and about 200 from South America, most of them from Colombia and Cuba. View image in fullscreen The opening ceremony of the Memorial Museum of Combat Feats at the Overseas Military Operations honouring North Korean troops killed while fighting for Russia, in Pyongyang in April. Photograph: KCNA/Reuters The records miss what is likely to be the deadliest foreign contingent of all. North Korea sent more than 10,000 troops to help Russia drive Ukrainian forces out of the Kursk region in late 2024 and 2025. South Korea’s national intelligence service estimates about 2,000 of them have been killed, and about 6,000 killed or wounded in total. The foreign soldiers arrived late. Of those whose date of death is recorded, three-quarters were killed in 2025 or later. Every Colombian death with a recorded date falls within that period, as recruiters turned to Latin America to make up for losses at home. No end in sight What the scale of the losses will mean for Russians’ attitudes to the war in the long run remains unclear. In interviews, many relatives of the dead said their grief had only hardened their support for the war. Several insisted that Russia must fight on, so that the sacrifice would not have been in vain. State propaganda has cast the fallen as heroes, holding up their deaths as a reason for Russians to stand united behind Putin and the army. The few who once spoke out against the war have mostly been jailed or forced to leave the country. The last group publicly protesting against the war, Put Domoi (Way Home), a movement of wives and mothers of mobilised men, was criminalised in 2024. One woman who was once among its most outspoken members said she now feared for her life. “I don’t have emotions any more; I am numb at this point. Just a question,” she asked rhetorically. “Is it worth it?” Explore more on these topics Russia’s war dead Russia Ukraine Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
